scenarios.title: Reuse a label printer
scenarios.summary: Turn repeated label output into a small reusable function.

initial.source:
# Repair the reusable printer; the caller already passes each label.
print_label() {
    printf 'Label: %s\n' "$2"
}
for label in "$@"; do
    print_label "$label"
done

cases.name: Empty label is still an argument

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on quoted arguments, for loops, printf and successful completion. No function knowledge is assumed.

concepts.title: A function names a reusable group of commands
concepts.text: A function lets you write a small job once and call it with different values. badge() { starts a definition; } ends it. Defining the function does not run its commands. Place its definition before its first call.

concepts.title: Each call gets its own arguments
concepts.text: badge Mina calls badge with one argument. Inside badge, $1 is Mina. A later badge call gets its own $1. When it finishes, the surrounding script gets its original positional arguments back.

concepts.title: Names and parameters are different
concepts.text: Function arguments are temporary, but ordinary named variables remain shared in this portable subset. Do not assume an assignment inside a function is private. Quote values at the call and inside the function. The final command supplies the function’s status.

teaching.inputs: No inputs or files are supplied. Two calls use Mina and Rowan Reed.
teaching.try_change: Change the second badge argument to a different two-word name and run again.

scenarios.retry_guidance: Compare labels across calls: a missing value may mean the function read the wrong positional argument; extra pieces usually mean a value was split.
scenarios.explanation: The loop supplies one label per call. That label becomes the function’s first argument; the surrounding argument list is restored after every call. A fixed printf format keeps percent signs in data harmless. An empty argument still creates one label line.

scenarios.title: Reject one item without ending the batch
scenarios.summary: Repair a helper so a bad item does not prevent later useful work.
scenarios.objective: For every label argument, print Accepted: LABEL plus a newline if it is nonempty. For an empty label print Rejected: empty label plus a newline to standard error, then continue to later labels. Finish with status 2 if any label was empty, otherwise 0; an empty batch succeeds with no output. Preserve values and all files. Repair the starter’s early termination.

initial.source:
accept_label() {
    if [ -z "$1" ]; then
        printf 'Rejected: empty label\n' >&2
        exit 2
    fi
    printf 'Accepted: %s\n' "$1"
}
failed=''
for label in "$@"; do
    if accept_label "$label"; then
        :
    else
        failed=yes
    fi
done
if [ -n "$failed" ]; then exit 2; fi
exit 0

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on function calls and the earlier batch failure flag. This lesson distinguishes return from exit.

concepts.title: Return ends this call; exit ends the script
concepts.text: A helper can reject one item without stopping the whole batch. return 1 leaves the function and gives the caller status 1. exit 1 ends the complete script, so later items never get a chance.

concepts.title: The caller decides how to continue
concepts.text: An if can call a function as its condition. Status 0 chooses then; nonzero chooses else. The caller can remember a failure and continue. return without a number uses the previous command’s status.

concepts.title: Batch status remembers earlier problems
concepts.text: A later successful item must not erase an earlier rejection. The shared failure flag records whether any item failed. The no-op : is a successful command for an intentionally empty branch.

teaching.example:
admit() {
    if [ -z "$1" ]; then
        printf 'Name needed\n' >&2
        return 1
    fi
    printf 'Welcome: %s\n' "$1"
}
admit ''
printf 'Still running\n'
admit Mina
teaching.inputs: No external inputs. The first call has an empty name and the second has Mina.
teaching.try_change: Change return 1 to exit 1 and run again. Does Still running appear?

scenarios.retry_guidance: If later labels disappear, inspect early exit. If output is right but status is 0 after a rejection, check whether a later success erased an earlier failure.
scenarios.explanation: return hands control back to the caller; it does not make the entire task successful. The caller handles every label and retains a failure flag. This separates an item’s result from the whole batch’s result.

    printf 'Prefix required\n' >&2

solution:
if [ -z "$1" ]; then
    printf 'Prefix required\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
prefix=$1
shift
for label in "$@"; do
    printf '%s: %s\n' "$prefix" "$label"
done

teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on positional arguments, quoted "$@", conditions and loops. This introduces shift.

concepts.title: Arguments can play different roles
concepts.text: A reusable program often receives one setting followed by several items. Save the setting before looping over the items. Otherwise the setting accidentally becomes an item too.

concepts.title: Shift removes leading positional arguments
concepts.text: shift removes the current $1: the old $2 becomes $1 and $# decreases by one. shift 2 removes two; shift 0 changes nothing. A count larger than the number of arguments fails with status 1 and leaves them unchanged in this Bash reference subset.

concepts.title: Preserve each remaining item
concepts.text: After consuming the header, "$@" still keeps every remaining argument separate, including a value containing spaces or an empty value. Inside a function, shift affects that function’s arguments; its caller’s arguments return unchanged when the function finishes.

teaching.example:
heading=$1
shift
for name in "$@"; do
    printf '%s: %s\n' "$heading" "$name"
done
printf 'Remaining=%s\n' "$#"
teaching.inputs: Arguments are Guest, Mina and Rowan Reed. No files are supplied.
teaching.try_change: Change shift to shift 0 and run again. Which extra item appears?

fixture.name: Consume a heading
fixture.stdout:
Guest: Mina
Guest: Rowan Reed
Remaining=2

scenarios.retry_guidance: If the prefix prints as a label, it was never removed from the item list. If words split or empty labels vanish, check the quoted argument vector.
scenarios.explanation: The first argument configures the output; it is not a label to print. Save it, consume it with shift, then iterate over the remaining quoted argument vector. Validating before consuming prevents missing input from being mistaken for a valid setting.

scenarios.title: Assemble a bundle only after preflight checks
scenarios.summary: Capstone: validate a batch before replacing an existing destination.
scenarios.objective: Argument 1 is a destination filename; all later arguments are source filenames in order. Require at least one source and check that every source exists before changing any file. On invalid input print Cannot assemble bundle plus a newline to standard error, return 2 and leave all files unchanged. On success replace the destination with Bundle plus a newline, then for each source append File: PATH plus a newline followed by its exact contents. Print Saved: DESTINATION plus a newline, return 0 and leave all other files unchanged. Inputs use nonempty ordinary filenames; the destination is different from every source.

initial.source:
validate_sources() {
    for source in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$source" ]; then
            :
        else
            return 2
        fi
    done
    return 0
}
if [ "$#" -lt 2 ]; then
    printf 'Cannot assemble bundle\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
destination=$1
shift
printf '' > "$destination"
if validate_sources "$@"; then
    printf 'Bundle\n' > "$destination"
    for source in "$@"; do
        printf 'File: %s\n' "$source" >> "$destination"
        cat "$source" >> "$destination"
    done
    printf 'Saved: %s\n' "$destination"
else
    printf 'Cannot assemble bundle\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi

teaching.prerequisite_note: Combines function return, shift, existence tests, loops and replacement/append. This lesson adds an argument-count guard before checking the source files.

concepts.title: Validate before changing the result
concepts.text: A failed job should not destroy the last useful report. Checking only the first source is insufficient: a later source could be missing. Finish the complete check before opening the destination with >.

concepts.title: Separate checking from writing
concepts.text: A helper can inspect all source arguments and return a status without changing files. The caller either reports a problem or builds the result. The example performs only the check, with different filenames.

concepts.title: Plan the replacement and append phases
concepts.text: Replace the destination once when validation succeeds, then append each heading and exact file contents in order. cat does not add a missing final line break. The complete assignment specifies the header and output channels.

concepts.title: Require enough arguments before preflight
concepts.text: "$#" is the number of supplied arguments, including empty ones. [ "$#" -lt 2 ] succeeds when that number is less than two; -lt compares whole numbers, unlike -z, which tests empty text. A destination plus at least one source needs two arguments. The example also receives two arguments, both source names, so its new guard lets the existing file check run. Guard the count before saving $1 and shifting in the assignment.

teaching.example:
if [ "$#" -lt 2 ]; then
    printf 'Need at least two example files\n' >&2
    exit 2
fi
available() {
    for file in "$@"; do
        if [ -f "$file" ]; then
            :
        else
            return 1
        fi
    done
    return 0
}
if available "$@"; then
    printf 'Ready to read\n'
else
    printf 'Nothing changed\n'
fi
teaching.inputs: Arguments are menu.txt and missing.txt: two supplied arguments, so the count guard passes. Only menu.txt exists with the text Soup plus a newline.
teaching.try_change: In the if available condition, replace "$@" with menu.txt and run again to observe the successful file check. Restore it, then change -lt 2 to -lt 3: the count guard rejects the two supplied arguments before preflight. Restore -lt 2 afterward; assignment drafts are separate.

scenarios.retry_guidance: If a failed test changed the destination, look for redirection before all input checks finished. If success differs, compare heading order, exact source contents and whether the destination was replaced only once.
scenarios.explanation: The destructive step is opening the destination with >. Complete validation first; only then replace the result and append source records. A failed preflight leaves the previous destination byte-for-byte intact. This models safe automation on virtual text files, not a real transactional filesystem.
